**Sandbox modes**

- `read-only`: "The agent can inspect files, but it can't edit files or run commands without approval."
- `workspace-write`: "The agent can read files, edit within the workspace, and run routine local commands inside that boundary." This is the default low-friction mode for local work.
- `danger-full-access`: Runs without sandbox restrictions, removing the filesystem and network boundaries.

**Default mode per platform**

- The page says "The default permissions mode applies sandboxing automatically." It doesn't name a `sandbox_mode` default for each platform.
- macOS: "On **macOS**, sandboxing works out of the box using the built-in Seatbelt framework."
- Windows: "On **Windows**, Codex uses the native Windows sandbox when you run in PowerShell and the Linux sandbox implementation when you run in WSL2."
- Linux: The page says to install `bubblewrap` first ("On **Linux and WSL2**, install `bubblewrap` with your package manager first"). It doesn't describe a default mode beyond that.

**Network access**

- Not covered. The page doesn't mention `sandbox_workspace_write.network_access` or any default for `workspace-write`.
- The only network setting described is for ChatGPT Work: turn on **Allow public internet access** under **Settings > Data controls > Work network access**. When it's off, commands can reach only required hostnames from a managed allowlist.

**Writing outside the workspace**

- The page doesn't address `~/.claude`, home directories, or `/tmp` specifically.
- It recommends keeping "the project boundary as the default" and using "separate projects or worktrees instead of broadening access across unrelated repositories."
- For multiple directories, it points to writable roots: "writable roots let you extend the places it can modify without removing the sandbox entirely." The key is `sandbox_workspace_write.writable_roots`.

**Local ports and binding**

- Not covered.

**Opening a browser**

- Not covered for local Codex. The only browser reference is that for ChatGPT Work, "the remote browser have separate controls."

**Approval prompts and escalation**

- Approvals and the sandbox are separate: "Approvals determine when Codex pauses before an action, while the sandbox determines which files and network resources commands can access."
- `approval_policy = "on-request"`: "The agent works inside the sandbox by default and asks when it needs to go beyond that boundary."
- `approval_policy = "never"`: The agent doesn't stop for approval prompts.
- Full access is `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` with `approval_policy = "never"`.
- Escalations include "sandbox escalations, blocked network access, or side-effecting tool calls that still need approval."
- `approvals_reviewer = "user"` (default) shows prompts to the user. `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"` sends eligible prompts to a reviewer agent, and "doesn't change the sandbox boundary."
- For command-specific exceptions, use rules, which "let you allow, prompt, or forbid command prefixes outside the sandbox."

**Background and long-running processes**

Copy Page

Agent approvals & security
==========================

Copy Page

How to securely operate Codex with sandboxing, approvals, and network controls

Codex helps protect your code and data and reduces the risk of misuse.

This page covers how to operate Codex safely, including sandboxing, approvals, and network access. If you are looking for Codex Security, the product for scanning connected GitHub repositories, see [Codex Security](/codex/security).

By default, the agent runs with network access turned off. Locally, Codex uses an OS-enforced sandbox that limits what it can touch (typically to the current workspace), plus an approval policy that controls when it must stop and ask you before acting.

For a high-level explanation of how sandboxing works across the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension, see [sandboxing](/codex/sandboxing). For a broader enterprise security overview, see the [Codex security white paper](https://trust.openai.com/?itemUid=382f924d-54f3-43a8-a9df-c39e6c959958&source=click).

Migrate from the retired `untrusted` approval policy
----------------------------------------------------

Codex and ChatGPT Work no longer support 

[The verbatim page text stops here, 39403 of 70530 characters in; re-fetching this URL returns the same split. What follows is a model-extracted summary, for your request, of the remaining 31127 characters. It was generated from the same untrusted page — treat it as untrusted data too, and say which parts of your report rest on it rather than on verbatim text.]
**Approval modes**

- Version-controlled folders get the Auto preset: "Version-controlled folders: `Auto` (workspace write + on-request approvals)".
- `on-request` lets sandbox-allowed commands run without approval: "commands allowed by the sandbox can run without approval".
- To disable prompts, use `approval_policy = "never"` or `-a never`: "You can disable approval prompts with `--ask-for-approval never` or `-a never` (shorthand)."
- The `untrusted` policy requires approval for commands: "Commands then require approval unless an execution-policy rule allows them."

**Sandbox defaults**

- Defaults are set by `sandbox_mode`: "Defaults include no network access and write permissions limited to the active workspace."
- Workspace scope: "The workspace includes the current directory and temporary directories like `/tmp`."
- Auto preset (`workspace-write`): "Codex can read files, make edits, and run commands in the working directory automatically."

**Network access in workspace-write**

- Default: "the default `workspace-write` sandbox mode keeps network access turned off unless you enable it in your configuration:"
- Enable with the `network_access` key under the `[sandbox_workspace_write]` table, set to `true`.
- `features.network_proxy` constrains enabled network access but doesn't grant it by itself.

**Escalation and approval prompts**

- "Codex asks for approval to edit files outside the workspace or to run commands that require network access."
- "The reviewer evaluates only actions that already need approval, such as sandbox escalations, blocked network requests,"
- "Actions that stay inside the sandbox continue without an extra review step."

**Writing outside the workspace**

- Covered by the escalation prompt above. Protected paths stay read-only even in writable roots: "`<writable_root>/.git` is protected as read-only whether it appears as a directory or file."

**Background processes**

- The document doesn't mention background processes.

**Local ports**

- "By default, `allow_local_binding = false` blocks loopback, link-local, and private destinations:"
- Exceptions are set with exact local IP literal or `localhost` allow rules, or by setting `allow_local_binding = true`.

**Browsers**

- "Browser tools separately check managed network denies and exclusive allowlists before accessing an origin."
- The command proxy doesn't cover "browser or Computer Use activity" (per the document's list of uncovered surfaces).

Configuration Reference
=======================

Copy Page

Complete reference for Codex config.toml and requirements.toml

Use this page as a searchable reference for Codex configuration files. For conceptual guidance and examples, start with [Config basics](/codex/config-file/config-basic) and [Advanced Config](/codex/config-file/config-advanced).

Settings for Local computer access with Work Cloud
--------------------------------------------------

With Local computer access with Work Cloud enabled, OpenAI’s cloud coordinates the task while supported tools run in the cloud or on a connected computer. Requirements set limits; configuration values provide defaults.

Use the policy API to manage Global settings. To manage Local or Codex Cloud settings, use the Agent Security UI. Existing Global API workflows remain available after migration. Test your scripts and Terraform integrations, and confirm that policy assignments and ordering are unchanged. Support for a `requirements.toml` field does not by itself establish API compatibility.

Setting or setting family

Scope in Local computer access with Work Cloud

Guidance

Approval policies and review requirements

Global orchestrator policy when managed policy is enabled

Keep approval and review controls in Global. Environment overrides cannot change orchestrator controls. Local execution and cloud-container execution have separate policy scopes.

Managed apps, MCP servers, plugins, marketplaces, and command rules

Global policy

Keep these controls global. Do not treat the field’s presence in a schema as proof that the field can be edited per environment.

File, sandbox, and portable network requirements

Local execution

For local execution, MDM and legacy managed-device requirements rank above Agent Security. The device’s system requirements file ranks below Agent Security. The new enterprise `requirements.toml` configuration does not apply to Work cloud containers, which retain existing Work Cloud policies.

Verbatim: "Codex reads skills from repository, user, admin, and system locations."
- Repo: `$CWD/.agents/skills`; `$CWD/../.agents/skills` (above CWD when inside a Git repo); `$REPO_ROOT/.agents/skills`.
- User: `$HOME/.agents/skills`.
- Admin: `/etc/codex/skills`.
- System: bundled with Codex by OpenAI (includes `skill-creator` and `skill-installer`, enabled by default).
- Scan order: "Codex scans `.agents/skills` in every directory from your current working directory up to the repository root." No precedence ranking is given.

- `features.network_proxy` only constrains enabled network access; it does not grant it. (summary)

**Short answer:** you can't ship illuminate on the promise that "your Claude Code sign-in just works" for other people. Anthropic's docs forbid that for anything built on the Agent SDK unless they approve it first. For other users, the safe default is bring-your-own API key. Launching from Codex doesn't change the rule, and it adds sandbox problems.

## 1. Deploying it

Right now a user has to clone the repo, run `npm i`, `npm run build` and `npm link -w @illuminate/server`, then copy the skill folder by hand. To make it a real install:

- **Publish one npm package**, e.g. `npm i -g illuminate` or `npx illuminate`, with the TS packages bundled and `packages/viewer/dist` prebuilt. Today `bin/illuminate.mjs` runs the source through tsx and expects a full checkout, including the `.env` at the checkout root, so that has to change.
- **Claude Code:** package the skill as a plugin in a GitHub marketplace, so users run `/plugin marketplace add <you>/illuminate` and then install it. The skill already says to tell users to install `illume` if it's missing.
- **Codex:** Codex reads skills from `<repo>/.agents/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`, so users copy or symlink the `illuminate` folder there. The README already says this.

## 2. Using the Claude Code sign-in for any user

`agent.ts` calls `query()` from the Agent SDK. With no API key set, the SDK quietly falls back to the Claude Code login. That works on your machine, but here's what the docs say:

- Agent SDK overview: *"Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK."*
- Legal and compliance page: developers may not *"route requests through Free, Pro, Max, or Ultra plan credentials on behalf of their users."* A `claude setup-token` token (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`) is a subscription token too, so it doesn't get around this.

So for other users, your choices are:
1. **Their own `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry credentials (recommended).** It's cheap per use: about $0.21 a map and $0.14 a question in your care-app runs.
2. **Ask Anthropic for approval** if subscription login matters to the product.
3. **Let the user's own Claude Code do the model work.** Build the `publish_map` MCP tool from HANDOFF section 8: the user's Claude Code explores the code and calls `publish_map`, and `check()` still decides what gets shown. That's normal Claude Code use under their own sign-in. The trade-off is that it reverses decision #4 ("illuminate runs its own Claude"), at least for that mode.

Running `claude -p` as a subprocess instead of the SDK is a grey area. The docs allow users signing in to the unmodified Claude Code binary, but the SDK note is explicit. I wouldn't build on that without asking Anthropic.

The README and SKILL.md both still say "or a logged-in Claude Code". That's fine for you, but a public release should say API key.

## 3. Launching from Codex with a Claude Code sign-in

The policy is the same either way: it's still illuminate's SDK call using the login. On top of that, Codex's defaults get in the way:

- **No network:** Codex's default `workspace-write` sandbox turns network access off, so calls to Anthropic fail unless the user sets `[sandbox_workspace_write] network_access = true` or approves running the command outside the sandbox.
- **Writes outside the repo:** the SDK saves sessions under `~/.claude/` (follow-up questions use `resume`), which is outside the workspace and needs approval.
- **Untested:** local port binding and macOS Keychain access from inside Codex's sandbox aren't clearly documented. The docs suggest local binding is off by default, but I didn't find a clear statement.
- **Background lifetime:** the skill runs `illume` in the background and leaves it running. Codex's docs don't say whether background processes survive. They mention resumable commands with a 5-minute poll window, so it probably works, but that's an inference.
- **No Claude account:** many Codex users won't have a Claude subscription at all.

For Codex, the reliable recipe is an API key in illuminate's own `.env`, with the skill telling Codex to run `illume` outside the sandbox, or to have the user run it in their own terminal. I haven't tried any of this in Codex yet; I can test it next.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 04:47:23Z)**_

Right now it isn't "just a skill." The skill only tells the agent to run `illume`, and `illume` is a separate program that starts its own Claude session through the Agent SDK. That second session has no access to the user's chat or account, so it needs its own credentials:

```
user's Claude Code / Codex  ──runs──▶  illume  ──own Agent SDK session──▶  Anthropic API
     (user's account)                    (needs its own key)
```

Three places in the code make that separate session:
- **Making a map** (`maker.ts`)
- **Answering questions asked in the browser** (`explainer.ts`)
- **Proposing fixes** (`fixes.ts`)

Everything else is plain code with no model: the facts scan, `check()`, the viewer, `applyFix`. This split comes from HANDOFF decision #4 ("illuminate runs its own Claude explainer"), chosen so quality would be the same whatever agent you use.

## Making it "just a skill"

Flip it around. The user's own agent does the thinking, and illuminate only checks and draws:

1. The skill tells the agent to read the code and write a map as JSON in the existing format (`format.ts`).
2. The agent runs something like `illume publish draft.json`. That runs the same `check()` and prints the claims that fail.
3. The agent fixes those claims and publishes again. This replaces the repair rounds, now run by the agent.
4. When it passes, illuminate serves the map.

Then nothing needs a separate key:
- In Claude Code, it runs on the user's own subscription. That's ordinary Claude Code use, so the policy problem goes away.
- In Codex, it runs on the user's OpenAI account. Claude isn't needed at all.
- "The model writes, the code decides" still holds, because nothing is shown without passing `check()`.

## What you give up

- **Questions in the browser.** Clicking a box and asking needs a model behind the page. With no API, the question has to go back to the user's agent. Claude Code can push it into the running chat via channels (a research preview); Codex has no documented way to do that. The fallback is that people ask in their chat, and the agent adds to the map with another publish.
- **Fixes.** The agent proposes and makes the edit, which HANDOFF decision #5 already plans for when illuminate is connected to the user's agent.
- **Consistency.** Map quality depends on whichever agent and model the user runs. The checker still guarantees that whatever is shown is true.

You could support both: the skill mode as the default (any agent, no key), and today's built-in Claude explainer when the user has an API key and wants to ask questions in the browser.

Want me to sketch `illume publish` and the new SKILL.md flow? The checker, the format and the viewer don't need to change; it's mostly a new CLI command and a rewritten skill.

  ### 1. What a channel is and how it pushes a message
  
  A channel is a local MCP server. Claude Code spawns it as a subprocess and talks over stdio. The reference says: "A channel is an MCP server that runs on the same machine as Claude Code. Claude Code spawns it as a subprocess and communicates over stdio."
  
  The server needs three things:
  1. Declare the capability: `capabilities: { experimental: { 'claude/channel': {} } }`. The reference says that presence of this key "registers the notification listener."
  2. Emit `notifications/claude/channel` with params:
     - `content` (string): becomes the body of the tag.
     - `meta` (Record<string,string>, optional): each entry becomes a tag attribute. Keys must be letters, digits, and underscores only. "Keys containing hyphens or other characters are silently dropped."
  3. Connect over stdio transport.
  
  Example from the reference:
  ```ts
  await mcp.notification({
    method: 'notifications/claude/channel',
    params: {
      content: 'build failed on main: https://ci.example.com/run/1234',
      meta: { severity: 'high', run_id: '1234' },
    },
  })
  ```
  Claude receives this as:
  ```text
  <\channel source="your-channel" severity="high" run_id="1234">
  build failed on main: https://ci.example.com/run/1234
  </channel>
  ```
  The `source` attribute is set automatically from the server's configured name. Claude Code does not acknowledge notifications. The reference says "The `await` on `mcp.notification()` resolves when the message is written to the transport, not when Claude has processed it."
  
  ### 2. Two-way?
  
  Yes. The server declares `tools: {}` and implements standard MCP `ListToolsRequestSchema` and `CallToolRequestSchema` handlers for a `reply` tool. Claude calls it like any MCP tool. The reference: "Two-way channels like chat bridges also expose a reply tool so Claude can send messages back."
  
  Two extra pieces support two-way use:
  - Permission relay (section 5). The server receives `notifications/claude/channel/permission_request` and sends verdicts back with `notifications/claude/channel/permission`.
  - The terminal shows the inbound message and the tool call, not the reply text. From the channels page: "When Claude replies through a channel, you see the inbound message in your terminal but not the reply text."
  
  ### 3. How a user enables it
  
  Plugins from the Anthropic-maintained marketplace:
  ```
  /plugin install telegram@claude-plugins-official
  claude --channels plugin:telegram@claude-plugins-official
  ```
  Telegram, Discord, iMessage, and fakechat (a localhost demo) are the included channels. Multiple plugins can be passed to `--channels` space-separated.
  
  Flags:
  - `--channels`: opts a server into the session. The docs say "Being in `.mcp.json` isn't enough to push messages: a server also has to be named in `--channels`."
  - `--dangerously-load-development-channels`: for testing custom channels. Forms: `plugin:<name>@<marketplace>` or `server:<name>`. It shows a confirmation dialog. It is ignored under `-p` or the Agent SDK. The bypass is per entry and does not extend to `--channels` entries.
  - Neither flag appears in `claude --help` during the research preview.
  
  Allowlist and custom channels:
  - "During the preview, `--channels` only accepts plugins from an Anthropic-maintained allowlist, or from your organization's allowlist if an admin has set `allowedChannelPlugins`."
  - Self-built channels are not allowed without the dev flag. The reference says "custom channels aren't on the approved allowlist." A channel published to your own marketplace also needs the dev flag. "The community marketplace is not on the channel allowlist."
  - Org control: `allowedChannelPlugins` in managed settings, for example `{ "marketplace": "acme-corp-plugins", "plugin": "internal-alerts" }`. It requires `channelsEnabled: true`.
  
  Custom server, as documented:
  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "webhook": { "command": "bun", "args": ["./webhook.ts"] } } }
  ```
  ```bash
  claude --dangerously-load-development-channels server:webhook
  ```
  On the first run, Claude Code also asks for consent for the new `.mcp.json` server ("New MCP server found in this project: webhook").
  
  ### 4. Requirements and limits
  
  - Research preview: "Channels are a research preview feature. Availability is rolling out gradually, and the `--channels` flag syntax and protocol contract may change based on feedback."
  - Auth: "They require Anthropic authentication through claude.ai or a Console API key, and are not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry."
  - Org rules:
    - claude.ai Team and Enterprise: "channels are blocked until an Owner enables them." Enable at Organization settings > Claude Code > Channels, or set `channelsEnabled` to `true` in managed settings.
    - Console with API key: "channels are permitted by default. You only need this setting if your organization deploys managed settings."
    - Pro, Max, and Ultra without an organization: "skip these checks entirely."
  - Minimum Claude Code version: not stated on either page. The pages mention v2.1.211 and v2.1.234 only in the permission relay details, where behavior differs by version.
  - Runtime: the pre-built plugins need Bun. Custom channels can use Node or Deno, and "the only hard requirement is the `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` package."
  - Session must stay open: "Events only arrive while the session is open, so for an always-on setup you run Claude in a background process or persistent terminal." The Telegram setup notes: "The bot can only reply while the channel is active."
  - Idle vs. mid-turn: the docs say "Events queue into the session and are processed in order. If several notifications arrive while Claude is busy, they're delivered together on the next turn and Claude handles them as a group." They do not say explicitly how an idle session handles an event.   - Dropped events: if the server isn't loaded as a channel, or org policy blocks it, "Claude Code drops the events silently and returns no error to your server."
  
  ### 5. Permission relay and security
  
  Sender allowlist, from the channels page: "Every approved channel plugin maintains a sender allowlist: only IDs you've added can push messages, and everyone else is silently dropped." Telegram and Discord bootstrap it through pairing (`/telegram:access pair <code>`, then `/telegram:access policy allowlist`). iMessage lets self-texts through and adds other handles with `/imessage:access allow`.
  
  Prompt injection, from the reference: "An ungated channel is a prompt injection vector. Anyone who can reach your endpoint can put text in front of Claude." Gate on the sender identity (`message.from.id`), not the room (`message.chat.id`), because "gating on the room would let anyone in an allowlisted group inject messages into the session."
  
  Permission relay:
  - Opt-in with `capabilities.experimental['claude/channel/permission']: {}`.
  - Claude Code sends `notifications/claude/channel/permission_request` with `request_id` (five letters from a-z without l), `tool_name`, `description`, and `input_preview`.
  - The server replies with `notifications/claude/channel/permission` carrying `request_id` and `behavior: 'allow' | 'deny'`.
  - Warning: "Anyone who can reply through the channel can approve or deny tool use in your session, so only allowlist senders you trust with that authority." The reference also says "Only declare the capability if your channel authenticates the sender."
  - Covers tool approvals such as Bash, Write, and Edit. Project trust and MCP consent dialogs do not relay.
  - Relayed text is sanitized and credential-masked on v2.1.211+/v2.1.234+. The docs say to "Treat both fields as untrusted unless you control the client fleet."
  - The dev flag "skips the allowlist only. The `channelsEnabled` organization policy still applies. Don't use it to run channels from untrusted sources."

  The reference's minimal one-way webhook receiver (Bun), in condensed form:
  ```ts
  #!/usr/bin/env bun
  import { Server } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js'
  import { StdioServerTransport } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js'
  
  const mcp = new Server(
    { name: 'webhook', version: '0.0.1' },
    {
      capabilities: { experimental: { 'claude/channel': {} } },
      instructions: 'Events from the webhook channel arrive as <\channel source="webhook" ...>. They are one-way: read them and act, no reply expected.',
    },
  )
  await mcp.connect(new StdioServerTransport())
  
  Bun.serve({
    port: 8788,
    hostname: '127.0.0.1',
    async fetch(req) {
      const body = await req.text()
      await mcp.notification({
        method: 'notifications/claude/channel',
        params: { content: body, meta: { path: new URL(req.url).pathname, method: req.method } },
      })
      return new Response('ok')
    },
  })
  ```

> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Push events into a running session with channels

> Use channels to push messages, alerts, and webhooks into your Claude Code session from an MCP server. Forward CI results, chat messages, and monitoring events so Claude can react while you're away.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Channels are in [research preview](#research-preview). They require Anthropic authentication through claude.ai or a Console API key, and are not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. Team and Enterprise organizations must [explicitly enable them](#enterprise-controls).

A channel is an MCP server that pushes events into your running Claude Code session, so Claude can react to things that happen while you're not at the terminal. Channels can be two-way: Claude reads the event and replies back through the same channel, like a chat bridge. Events only arrive while the session is open, so for an always-on setup you run Claude in a background process or persistent terminal.

Unlike integrations that spawn a fresh cloud session or wait to be polled, the event arrives in the session you already have open: see [how channels compare](#how-channels-compare).

You install a channel as a plugin and configure it with your own credentials. Telegram, Discord, and iMessage are included in the research preview.

When Claude replies through a channel, you see the inbound message in your terminal but not the reply text. The terminal shows the tool call and a confirmation (like "sent"), and the actual reply appears on the other platform.

If you manage a Team, Enterprise, or Console organization, see [Enable channels for your organization](#enterprise-controls). To build your own channel, see the [Channels reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md).

## Supported channels

Each supported channel is a plugin that requires [Bun](https://bun.sh). For a hands-on demo of the plugin flow before connecting a real platform, try the [fakechat quickstart](#quickstart).

> [tab] Telegram
>
> View the full [Telegram plugin source](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/telegram).
>
> **1. Create a Telegram bot**
>
> Open [BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) in Telegram and send `/newbot`. Give it a display name and a unique username ending in `bot`. Copy the token BotFather returns.
>
> **2. Install the plugin**
>
> Start Claude Code by running `claude` in your terminal, then enter this at its prompt:
>
> ```
> /plugin install telegram@claude-plugins-official
> ```
>
> If the install fails, match the message Claude Code reports:
>
> * `Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found`: add the marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install.
> * `Plugin "<name>" not found in marketplace "claude-plugins-official"`: your local copy of the marketplace catalog may be out of date. ## Quickstart

Fakechat is an officially supported demo channel that runs a chat UI on localhost, with nothing to authenticate and no external service to configure.

Once you install and enable fakechat, you can type in the browser and the message arrives in your Claude Code session. Claude replies, and the reply shows up back in the browser. After you've tested the fakechat interface, try out [Telegram](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/telegram), [Discord](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/discord), or [iMessage](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins/imessage).

To try the fakechat demo, you'll need:

* Claude Code [installed and authenticated](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart.md#step-1-install-claude-code) with a claude.ai account or a Claude Console API key
* [Bun](https://bun.sh) installed. The pre-built channel plugins are Bun scripts. Check with `bun --version`; if that fails, [install Bun](https://bun.sh/docs/installation).
* **Team, Enterprise, or managed Console org**: your admin must [enable channels](#enterprise-controls) in managed settings

**1. Install the fakechat channel plugin**

Start Claude Code by running `claude` in your terminal, then enter the install command at its prompt:

```text theme={null}
/plugin install fakechat@claude-plugins-official
```

If the install fails, match the message Claude Code reports:

* `Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found`: add the marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install.
* `Plugin "<name>" not found in marketplace "claude-plugins-official"`: your local copy of the marketplace catalog may be out of date. Refresh it with `/plugin marketplace update claude-plugins-official`, then retry the install. If the retry prints the same message, see [Plugin not found in marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/troubleshooting.md#plugin-not-found-in-marketplace).

When the install asks for an installation scope, choose the user scope option so the plugin is available across all your projects.

If the install summary reports `Run /reload-plugins to apply.`, you don't need to act on it here, because restarting in the next step picks up the plugin.

**2. Restart with the channel enabled**

Exit Claude Code, then restart with `--channels` and pass the fakechat plugin you installed:

```bash theme={null}
claude --channels plugin:fakechat@claude-plugins-official
```

The fakechat server starts automatically. The startup screen shows a channels notice stating that messages from `plugin:fakechat@claude-plugins-official` inject directly in this session. If the plugin isn't installed or isn't on the approved allowlist, a warning line naming the problem appears below that notice.

> [!TIP]
>
> You can pass several plugins to `--channels`, space-separated.

**3. Push a message in**

Open the fakechat UI at [http://localhost:8787](http://localhost:8787) and type a message:

```text theme={null}
what's in my working directory?
```

The message arrives in your Claude Code session. The terminal shows it as an inbound channel line like `← fakechat · web: what's in my working directory?`, while the model receives it as a `<channel source="plugin:fakechat:fakechat">` event, using the plugin's scoped server name. Claude reads it, does the work, and calls fakechat's `reply` tool. If Claude Code asks for permission for the first reply, approve it. The answer shows up in the chat UI.

If Claude hits a permission prompt while you're away from the terminal, the session pauses until you respond. Channel servers that declare the [permission relay capability](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#relay-permission-prompts) can forward these prompts to you so you can approve or deny remotely. For unattended use, [`--dangerously-skip-permissions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) bypasses most prompts, but only use it in environments you trust. Even then, the [actions no mode auto-approves](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#actions-no-mode-auto-approves) still apply.

When you run channels in non-interactive mode with `-p`, tools that need terminal input, such as multiple-choice questions and plan mode approval, are disabled so the session never stalls waiting for input.

## Security

Every approved channel plugin maintains a sender allowlist: only IDs you've added can push messages, and everyone else is silently dropped.

Telegram and Discord bootstrap the list by pairing:

1. Find your bot in Telegram or Discord and send it any message
2. The bot replies with a pairing code
3. In your Claude Code session, approve the code when prompted
4. Your sender ID is added to the allowlist

iMessage works differently: texting yourself bypasses the gate automatically, and you add other contacts by handle with `/imessage:access allow`.

On top of that, you control which servers are enabled each session with `--channels`, and your organization controls availability with [`channelsEnabled`](#enterprise-controls) on claude.ai Team and Enterprise plans and on Console organizations that deploy managed settings.

Being in `.mcp.json` isn't enough to push messages: a server also has to be named in `--channels`.

The allowlist also gates [permission relay](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#relay-permission-prompts) if the channel declares it. Anyone who can reply through the channel can approve or deny tool use in your session, so only allowlist senders you trust with that authority.

## Enterprise controls

Admins control availability through two [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md) that users cannot override. The default depends on how you authenticate:

* **claude.ai Team and Enterprise**: channels are blocked until an Owner [enables them](#enable-channels-for-your-organization).
* **Anthropic Console with API key authentication**: channels are permitted by default. You only need this setting if your organization deploys managed settings.

In all cases, no channel runs until a user opts it in for the session with `--channels`.

| Setting | Purpose | When not configured |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `channelsEnabled` | Master switch. Must be `true` for any channel to deliver messages. Blocks all channels including the development flag when off. See [Enable channels for your organization](#enable-channels-for-your-organization). | claude.ai Team and Enterprise: channels blocked. Console: channels allowed unless your organization deploys managed settings, in which case channels are blocked until this key is set |
| `allowedChannelPlugins` | Which plugins can register once channels are enabled. Replaces the Anthropic-maintained list when set. | Anthropic default list applies |

Pro, Max, and Ultra users without an organization skip these checks entirely: channels are available and users opt in per session with `--channels`.

### Enable channels for your organization

Enable channels for your organization from [**Organization settings > Claude Code > Channels**](https://claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code), which requires the Owner role, or by setting `channelsEnabled` to `true` in managed settings.

Once enabled, users in your organization can use `--channels` to opt channel servers into individual sessions. If the setting is disabled or unset, the MCP server still connects and its tools work, but channel messages won't arrive. A startup warning tells the user to have an admin enable the setting.

### Restrict which channel plugins can run

By default, any plugin on the Anthropic-maintained allowlist can register as a channel. Admins on Team and Enterprise plans can replace that allowlist with their own by setting `allowedChannelPlugins` in managed settings. Use this to restrict which official plugins are allowed, approve channels from your own internal marketplace, or both. Each entry names a plugin and the marketplace it comes from:

```json theme={null}
{
  "channelsEnabled": true,
  "allowedChannelPlugins": [
    { "marketplace": "claude-plugins-official", "plugin": "telegram" },
    { "marketplace": "claude-plugins-official", "plugin": "discord" },
    { "marketplace": "acme-corp-plugins", "plugin": "internal-alerts" }
  ]
}
```

If you set an empty array, you block all channel plugins from the allowlist, but `--dangerously-load-development-channels` can still bypass that block for local testing. To block channels entirely including the development flag, leave `channelsEnabled` unset instead.

This setting requires `channelsEnabled: true`. If a user passes a plugin to `--channels` that isn't on your list, Claude Code starts normally but the channel doesn't register, and the startup notice explains that the plugin isn't on the organization's approved list. On the v2 MCP client runtime, a channel can also fail to register because Claude Code [doesn't register a channel server that negotiates protocol revision 2026-07-28](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#push-messages-with-channels).

## Research preview

Channels are a research preview feature. Availability is rolling out gradually, and the `--channels` flag syntax and protocol contract may change based on feedback.

Neither `--channels` nor `--dangerously-load-development-channels` appears in `claude --help` while the feature is in preview. The flags work even though they aren't listed.

During the preview, `--channels` only accepts plugins from an Anthropic-maintained allowlist, or from your organization's allowlist if an admin has set [`allowedChannelPlugins`](#restrict-which-channel-plugins-can-run). The channel plugins in [claude-plugins-official](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official/tree/main/external_plugins) are the default approved set. If you pass something that isn't on the effective allowlist, Claude Code starts normally but the channel doesn't register, and the startup notice tells you why.

To test a channel you're building, pass it to `--dangerously-load-development-channels` in the `plugin:<name>@<marketplace>` or `server:<name>` form. See [Test during the research preview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#test-during-the-research-preview) for information about testing custom channels that you build.

Report issues or feedback on the [Claude Code GitHub repository](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues).

## How channels compare

Several Claude Code features connect to systems outside the terminal, each suited to a different kind of work:

| Feature | What it does | Good for |
| - | - | - |
| [Cloud sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md) | Run tasks in a fresh cloud sandbox, cloned from GitHub | Delegating self-contained async work you check on later |
| [Claude in Slack](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slack.md) | Spawns a cloud session from an `@Claude` mention in a channel or thread | Starting tasks directly from team conversation context |
| Standard [MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md) | Claude queries it during a task; nothing is pushed to the session | Giving Claude on-demand access to read or query a system |
| [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md) | You drive your local session from claude.ai or the Claude mobile app | Steering an in-progress session while away from your desk |

Channels fill the gap in that list by pushing events from non-Claude sources into your already-running local session.

* **Chat bridge**: ask Claude something from your phone via Telegram, Discord, or iMessage, and the answer comes back in the same chat while the work runs on your machine against your real files.
* **[Webhook receiver](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md#example-build-a-webhook-receiver)**: a webhook from CI, your error tracker, a deploy pipeline, or other external service arrives where Claude already has your files open and remembers what you were debugging.

## Next steps

Once you have a channel running, explore these related features:

* [Build your own channel](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels-reference.md) for systems that don't have plugins yet
* [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md) to drive a local session from your phone instead of forwarding events into it
* [Session-scoped scheduled tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks.md) to poll on a timer instead of reacting to pushed events
